purpose: Adds an opt-in (default off) Server-Timing response header on WP 6.9+ live front-end renders measuring request bootstrap and template-render durations via the template-enhancement output-buffer hooks, plus a null-safe REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT accessor in System_Info.
riskRationale: The feature itself is small, well-guarded, and safe when disabled, but the commit also bundles ~4,737 dev-only Composer packages (~525K lines: phpunit, phpcs, mockery, brain/monkey, patchwork, etc.) into the tracked vendor/ tree, violating the documented production-only vendor workflow and risking dev tooling shipping to WordPress.org if any release path skips the --no-dev reinstall.
breakingChanges: vendor/ must be regenerated production-only via composer release before merge; the committed dev-dependency tree must be stripped from the tracked vendor/ directory

text: The Server-Timing feature is cleanly implemented: opt-in default-off, version-guarded on the WP 6.9 hook, isolated to two defensively-guarded callbacks, with a tidy null-safe REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT helper in System_Info. The blocking problem is scope creep — the commit bundles ~4,700 dev-only vendor files (~525K lines) in violation of the documented composer release workflow — and the remaining work is several minor items: the wp-before-template metric overlaps wp-template, server_timing_enabled can be silently wiped by update_settings, and the PR description makes inaccurate claims about setting defaults and a filter hook.

reasoning: Feature code is sound and backward-compatible, but vendor/ must be regenerated production-only via composer release and update_settings must preserve server_timing_enabled before merge. Both fixes are mechanical and carry no regression risk.

message: Hook registration is cleanly gated on both the WP 6.9 function_exists() check and the new default-off setting, kept independent of enableCache, so there is zero behavior change for existing installs and no hooks registered when disabled.

get_request_start_microtime() centralizes the sanitized $_SERVER access into a static, null-safe, typed (?float) helper with a targeted phpcs:ignore, returning null on CLI/cron and rejecting non-positive values.

Both callbacks carry belt-and-suspenders is_admin()/wp_doing_ajax()/REST_REQUEST guards plus a headers_sent() check immediately before header(), and were verified against WP core semantics (the action's $output parameter is safe and core wraps callbacks in try/catch), so the emitter cannot corrupt a partially-sent response.

This commit adds ~4,737 files / ~525K lines of dev-only Composer dependencies to the tracked vendor/ directory (phpunit, squizlabs/php_codesniffer, wp-coding-standards/wpcs, antecedent/patchwork, brain/monkey, mockery, nikic/php-parser, sebastian/*, phar-io/*, vendor/bin, etc.) and rewrites vendor/composer/installed.json, installed.php and autoload_* to reference them, while composer.json/composer.lock were not changed. This directly violates AGENTS.md, which mandates running `composer release` (composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader) before `git add vendor/` so only production deps (voku/html-min, matthiasmullie/minify, woocommerce/action-scheduler) ship. It bloats git history by hundreds of thousands of lines, inflates the committed autoloader (which Main::includes() requires on every request), and because .distignore only excludes a subset of these packages, any release path that skips a fresh --no-dev install would ship PHPUnit/PHPCS/Patchwork to production WordPress installs.
suggestion: Regenerate the vendor tree in production mode and re-commit only production dependencies: run `composer release` (composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader --ignore-platform-reqs), verify `git status vendor/` no longer lists dev packages, then commit vendor/ with the PHP changes only. Do not commit the output of a dev-setup install.
suggestionCode: composer release && git add vendor/ && git status vendor/

message: update_settings() does $options[$tab] = $sanitized_settings, replacing the whole performance_audit array with whatever the client sends. Because the PR intentionally adds no UI toggle, the React app never sends server_timing_enabled, so a user who enables it via import_settings or WP-CLI will have it silently wiped back to false the next time the Performance Audit tab is saved. pagespeed_api_key had the identical problem and got a dedicated preservation guard at class-rest.php:383-385; server_timing_enabled needs the same treatment.
suggestion: Mirror the pagespeed_api_key guard: when the tab is performance_audit and the request omits server_timing_enabled, preserve the stored value before replacing the tab array.

message: The wp-before-template metric is mislabeled: it is computed as (now - REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT) at the finalize hook, which fires AFTER the template has rendered, so it measures total request duration and fully overlaps the separately-reported wp-template render time. This contradicts the PR's stated goal of measuring 'bootstrap-to-template-start', and the name collides with the de-facto Server-Timing convention (Performance Lab's wp-before-template), where browsers merge same-named entries with last-wins — so this value could silently overwrite a standard one on coexisting sites.
suggestion: Compute wp-before-template from the captured template-start marker (server_timing_template_start) instead of the finalize timestamp so the two metrics are disjoint and correctly named, falling back to the total when the marker is missing.

message: The PR description contains inaccurate claims. First, 'existing serialized settings are merged with defaults by WordPress' is wrong — get_option( 'wppo_settings', $defaults ) returns the stored array as-is and does not deep-merge missing keys; the code is safe only because of the `?? false` null-coalescing guard. Second, the description says the setting can be enabled 'via a filter', but no filter hook exists anywhere in the code — only import_settings/WP-CLI can flip it.
suggestion: Keep the `?? false` guard (it is what actually provides the backward-compatible default) but correct the PR description to state the default relies on `?? false`/`! empty()`, not WordPress merging serialized defaults, and either add a small filter (e.g. apply_filters( 'wppo_server_timing_enabled', $enabled )) or remove the filter claim.

message: header() uses PHP's default replace semantics, so if another plugin or a reverse proxy already set a Server-Timing header earlier in the request, this call silently overwrites it and that timing data is lost. For an additive opt-in debug header, appending is more courteous to coexisting tooling.
suggestion: Use append mode so existing timing entries are preserved: header( 'Server-Timing: ' . implode( ', ', $timings ), false ).

message: The new telemetry code paths have no automated coverage: neither the happy path (well-formed header emission with both metrics) nor the bail-outs (headers_sent, null REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT, admin/AJAX/REST, setting off). This is consistent with the repo having no PHP unit-test infrastructure, but composer.json already wires phpunit + brain/monkey so a focused test would be low-effort for this deterministic logic.
suggestion: Add a smoke test (e.g. brain/monkey-based) that mocks $_SERVER['REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT'], invokes emit_server_timing_header(), and asserts the header string and the admin/AJAX/REST early-return guards; at minimum note manual verification steps in the PR.

message: emit_server_timing_header( $output ) declares a parameter that is never used and suppresses the WPCS unused-parameter warning with a phpcs:ignore comment. Minor cleanup: register the callback with zero accepted args and drop the parameter.
suggestion: Register as add_action( 'wp_finalized_template_enhancement_output_buffer', array( $this, 'emit_server_timing_header' ), 0, 0 ) and change the signature to emit_server_timing_header(): void, removing the phpcs:ignore comment.

message: When the setting is enabled, the Server-Timing header is emitted to every visitor including anonymous users, exposing backend bootstrap and template-render latency to unauthenticated clients. This is intended opt-in telemetry, but it is easy to forget to disable in production.
suggestion: Consider emitting only for logged-in users with manage_options capability (or behind an opt-in filter) to limit information disclosure, and document the setting in the audit tab.

message: Per WP 6.9 core semantics, merely adding a wp_finalized_template_enhancement_output_buffer action causes the enhancement output buffer to be started automatically for every template (wp_should_output_buffer_template_for_enhancement() returns true because of the registered action). Enabling this debug feature therefore forces full-output buffering of live renders, disabling response streaming and increasing TTFB — the exact trade-off the WP 6.9 field guide warns about.
suggestion: Document the streaming trade-off in the feature docs/readme/setting description so operators know enabling the setting disables response streaming.

message: Because the emit hook is registered regardless of the page-cache setting, the header is present only on cache-miss generation passes when the static HTML cache is enabled; already-cached responses served by advanced-cache.php never boot WordPress and carry no header. A user enabling this for diagnostics will see the header intermittently, which can be confusing when comparing timings across requests.
suggestion: Document this limitation in the setting description, or skip header emission when the response is being stored to the page cache so the dataset is consistent.
